A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same GenzIQA research, with v2 extending it to video quality assessment. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and support a reliable comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original cross-database and intra-database IQA results, component ablations, and generated-image experiments, including those in the appendices.

after.justification: v2 retains original IQA experiments and reports additional video-quality benchmarks, temporal-modulator ablations, backbone comparisons, and cross-database generated-image results.

M1.justification: v2 retains the core GenzIQA attention, prompt-learning, and pooling design but introduces GenzVQA. Section 3.3 adds one-frame-per-second quality estimation and a temporal quality modulator combining diffusion features with SlowFast features. Video training also updates query weights, which remain frozen for IQA.

E1.justification: v2 adds video assessment using LSVQ training and eleven cross-database evaluation datasets covering camera captures, frame-rate variation, Ultra-HD, gaming, and streaming. IQA coverage additionally includes SPAQ, TID2013, KADID-10K, and AIGIQA-20K. The three generated-image evaluation datasets from v1 remain represented.

E2.justification: Table 1 adds ARNIQA, QCN, and partial DP-IQA/PFD-IQA comparisons. Intra-database IQA adds LIQE, ARNIQA, QPT, QCN, LoDA, and DSMix; Appendix A.4 also directly compares LIQE under matched training data. New video comparisons include VSFA, DOVER, and ModularVQA, while generated-image comparisons add CLIP-IQA+ and IPCE.

E3.justification: The reported IQA training budget changes from 15 to 10 epochs, and inference changes from averaging eight sampled timesteps to using fixed t=50. Generated-image evaluation changes from within-dataset 80:20 splits to AIGIQA-20K training and external-dataset testing. New video protocols specify six training epochs, sparse frame processing, LSVQ training, and dataset-specific finetuning. These descriptions do not establish that retained results were rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds controlled tests of SlowFast features versus motion cross-attention, video query-weight learning, Stable Diffusion v1.5 versus v2, distortion separability after resizing/VAE processing, and two video correction case studies. Existing prompt, resolution, denoising-step, and IQA component analyses are largely retained or relocated rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: v1 Appendix B explicitly uses ten random splits for generated-image evaluation; its replacement in v2 Appendix A.5 specifies an official training split without reporting repeated-run estimation. Retained intra-dataset IQA still reports medians over ten splits, and video finetuning follows that existing practice. Neither version supplies confidence intervals, seed variability, or significance tests.

E6.justification: v2 adds extensive video, LIQE, backbone, and generated-image cross-database results. Reported intra-database GenzIQA SRCC/PLCC changes from 0.916/0.932 to 0.936/0.950 on KonIQ and from 0.613/0.718 to 0.627/0.728 on FLIVE. Original Table 1 dataset scores and many ablation values remain unchanged. Revised training/inference descriptions and replacement generated-image protocols prevent treating all numerical differences as same-setting improvements.

T1.justification: Section 3.3 adds mathematical definitions for sparse-video averaging, motion cross-attention, temporal modulation, and the final video score. The underlying diffusion and IQA mathematics remains equivalent, while v1's LoRA factorization is omitted. The additions formulate the new procedure without introducing theoretical guarantees or proofs.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion expand the central contribution from generalized IQA to a unified image/video framework. A novel temporal quality modulator and computationally practical video assessment become explicit contributions. v1's separate contribution emphasizing adaptation with very few parameters is no longer stated.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations of motion loss from subsampling, temporal correction, video query-weight learning, paired-prompt behavior, and preservation of distortion information through resizing and the VAE. It removes v1's explicit aspect-ratio limitation and adds edge-device and higher-resolution compute limitations. The difficulty of assessing PIPAL images remains acknowledged.

D1.justification: v2 adds a repository pointer, SlowFast pretraining and feature-dimension details, temporal-modulator implementation information, the number of diffusion cross-attention blocks, and dataset metadata tables. It also reports video runtime and parameter counts. Conversely, v1's explicit LoRA adaptation description disappears; the PDFs do not explain whether that implementation was abandoned.

R1.justification: Related work expands substantially into video quality assessment and positions GenzVQA against feature-based, transformer, and vision-language approaches. IQA positioning now explicitly discusses recent diffusion methods such as DP-IQA, PFD-IQA, and DiffV2IQA, including differences in adaptation and computational cost.

P1.justification: The introduction, contribution list, method narrative, and conclusion are extensively rewritten around image and video assessment. Related work is reorganized into IQA/VQA sections, analyses are consolidated under Section 4.4, and several studies move between the main text and appendices. The title and author information also change.

P2.justification: v2 redraws the main architecture diagram, adds a temporal-modulator diagram and distortion-specific visualizations, expands benchmark tables, and introduces video, efficiency, and dataset-summary tables. Existing figures and tables are also relocated or reformatted, including rearranging the noise plots and correcting the fixed-prompt column labels from v1 Table 10.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation of the central generalization claim: it supplies the previously missing LIQE comparison, replaces within-dataset generated-image testing with cross-dataset evaluation, and examines the video extension through component ablations and computational comparisons. These address important gaps in comparative and mechanistic evidence. The gains outweigh lost LoRA documentation and reporting weaknesses, including unexplained Table 1 averages and broad superiority wording that overlooks dataset-specific losses such as LIVE-IQA and LIVE-YT-Gaming.
